rewritten_text:
With no work left in his hands, he pressed the knuckles of his right hand into his left palm, then his left knuckles into his right palm, then rubbed a hand across his bearded chin. He repeated these movements in a steady sequence, never pausing. After speaking, he always drifted into a distracted state. Bringing him back from it was like waking someone terribly weak from a faint, or trying to hold back a dying man's spirit in the hope of hearing some final revelation.

“Did you ask my name?”

“Yes, I certainly did.”

“One Hundred and Five, North Tower.”

“Is there nothing more?”

“One Hundred and Five, North Tower.”

Making a weary sound that was neither a sigh nor a groan, he bent over his work again, until someone broke the silence once more.

“Shoemaking isn't your profession?” Mr. Lorry asked, watching him steadily.

His exhausted eyes turned toward Defarge, as though he hoped Defarge would answer for him. Finding no help there, he looked down at the floor, then back at the man who had asked.

“Shoemaking isn't my profession? No, I wasn't a shoemaker. I—I learned it here. I taught myself. I asked permission to—”

He drifted away again, this time for minutes, keeping up the same measured movements of his hands. At last his eyes slowly returned to the face they had left. When they settled on it, he gave a start and continued speaking, like someone just awakened who returns to a conversation from the night before.

“I asked permission to teach myself. After a long time, and with great difficulty, I got it. I've been making shoes ever since.”

He reached for the shoe that had been taken from him. Still looking steadily into his face, Mr. Lorry said:

“Monsieur Manette, do you remember nothing about me?”

The shoe fell to the floor. He sat staring at the man who had spoken.

“Monsieur Manette,” Mr. Lorry said, placing his hand on Defarge's arm, “do you remember nothing about this man? Look at him. Look at me. Does no old banker come to mind? No former business, no old servant, no earlier time, Monsieur Manette?”

The man who had spent so many years imprisoned sat staring from Mr. Lorry to Defarge and back again. Gradually, lines appeared in the center of his forehead, signs of an alert, concentrated mind that had long been erased. They struggled through the dark fog that had settled over him. Then the fog covered them again; they faded and vanished. But they had been there.

His manner was stubborn to the last degree, and throughout the journey nothing passed his lips except “dat deuced bug.” I myself had undertaken to carry two dark lanterns; Legrand wanted only the scarabæus, which hung from a short piece of whipcord and which he swung about as he walked, with the manner of a magician. Seeing this final, unmistakable sign of my friend's mental derangement, I could barely keep back my tears. Nevertheless, I judged it wisest to indulge his whim for the moment, or at least until firmer measures might promise some success. Meanwhile I tried, quite fruitlessly, to discover the purpose of our expedition. Once he had persuaded me to join him, he seemed disinclined to discuss any lesser subject, and answered every inquiry with nothing beyond “we shall see!”

We took a skiff across the creek at the island's head, climbed the rising ground along the mainland shore, and made our way northwest through a district of extraordinary wilderness and desolation, without a visible trace of human footsteps. Legrand advanced with assurance, stopping only briefly from time to time to examine what seemed to be landmarks he had established on an earlier visit.

We continued thus for some two hours. The sun was going down when we reached a place far more dismal than any we had yet encountered. It was a kind of plateau near the crest of an almost unscalable hill, covered from foot to summit in dense woods. Immense crags lay scattered among the trees, seemingly loose upon the earth; many appeared to be kept from plunging into the valleys beneath solely by the trees against which they rested. Deep gullies running in several directions lent the scene an even graver and more forbidding solemnity.

The natural terrace we had climbed to was so densely covered in brambles that we soon found it would have been impossible to press through them without the scythe. At his master's instruction, Jupiter began cutting a passage to the base of a tulip-tree of enormous height. It stood on the level ground with eight or ten oaks, surpassing every one of them—and every other tree I had ever seen—in the loveliness of its shape and foliage, the breadth of its spreading limbs, and the stately grandeur of its whole appearance.

Jupiter could hardly contain his joy at the sight of these things, but his master's face showed bitter disappointment. Still, he urged us to keep working. The words were barely out of his mouth when the toe of my boot caught in a large iron ring half buried in the loose soil, and I tripped and fell forward.

Now we dug in earnest. I have never experienced ten minutes of greater excitement. In that time we uncovered a rectangular wooden chest. Its remarkable hardness and perfect condition showed that it had been treated with some mineral preservative, perhaps mercury bichloride. It measured three and a half feet long, three feet wide, and two and a half feet deep. Riveted bands of wrought iron held it firmly together, forming an open lattice over its entire surface. Near the top were three iron rings on each side, six altogether, allowing six people to take a solid grip. Even with all our strength combined, we could barely shift the chest in its hollow. We immediately understood that we could not move such a weight. Fortunately, only two sliding bolts held down the lid. Trembling and breathing hard with anticipation, we slid them back. In an instant, treasure beyond calculation glittered before us. As the lantern light reached into the pit, a blaze of reflected light shot up from a jumbled heap of gold and jewels, dazzling our eyes.

I will not attempt to describe everything I felt as I stared. Amazement, of course, overwhelmed the rest. Legrand seemed worn out by excitement and hardly spoke. For several minutes Jupiter's face turned as deathly pale as his dark skin could possibly become. He appeared stunned, struck speechless. Then he dropped to his knees in the pit and plunged his bare arms into the gold up to his elbows. He left them there as though enjoying the luxury of a bath. At last he gave a deep sigh and said, seemingly to himself:

“And all this came from the gold-bug! The pretty gold-bug! The poor little gold-bug that I treated so cruelly! Aren't you ashamed of yourself, you black fool? Answer me that!”

Eventually I had to rouse both master and servant and remind them that we should carry the treasure away. It was getting late, and we needed to work hard if we meant to have everything indoors before daylight. None of us could easily decide how to proceed. Our thoughts were so confused that we spent a great deal of time discussing what to do.
